name: Underhook Recovery
description: Learn Underhook Recovery from Double Unders bottom in BJJ. Recover defensive underhook to disrupt pressure passing. Success rates: Beginner 25%, Intermediate 45%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
Underhook Recovery from Double Unders bottom is a critical defensive transition that addresses one of the most pressing problems in pressure passing defense: regaining structural integrity when both underhooks have been conceded. When the top player establishes double underhooks beneath your legs, your entire guard framework collapses — leg pummeling is neutralized, frames become ineffective against stacking pressure, and the pass completion window shrinks rapidly. The underhook recovery targets the root cause by fighting to thread one arm inside the top player's control loop, wedging your forearm between their bicep and your thigh to break the bilateral grip and restore asymmetric engagement.

The technique operates on a fundamental principle: double underhooks derive their power from symmetry. The top player's crushing pressure depends on both arms working in concert to compress your legs together and stack your hips. By recovering even a single underhook on one side, you break this symmetry entirely. The recovered underhook creates a wedge that prevents re-consolidation of the double unders grip, gives you a posting arm to generate hip escape angles, and opens space for knee shield or butterfly hook insertion on the freed side.

Strategically, underhook recovery sits between passive acceptance of the pass and explosive escape attempts like granby rolls or deep half entries. It requires less commitment than those options while providing a structured pathway back to viable guard positions. Advanced practitioners chain underhook recovery with immediate hip escapes to half guard or butterfly hook reinsertions, treating the recovered underhook as the first link in a guard retention sequence rather than an endpoint.
key_principles: Target the weaker side of the double underhook grip — the arm with shallower penetration or looser elbow connection offers the best recovery opportunity
Use skeletal frames rather than muscular pushing — bone-on-bone contact between your forearm and their bicep generates sustainable separation force
Time the recovery attempt to coincide with the top player's weight shifts or grip adjustments when pressure momentarily lightens
The recovered underhook must immediately translate to hip movement — the underhook alone is insufficient without creating an escape angle
Maintain constant elbow-to-hip connection on the recovery side to prevent the top player from re-establishing the underhook
Chain the recovery directly into guard recomposition — half guard knee shield or butterfly hook insertion must follow within one to two seconds
Control the wrist or bicep of the arm you displaced to prevent immediate re-pummel back to double unders
setup_requirements: Opponent has established double underhooks beneath your legs with hands connected behind your back or gripping belt
At least one arm is free to initiate the recovery — not trapped beneath your own body or pinned by opponent's head pressure
Sufficient hip angle to create insertion space — you must be turned slightly to one side rather than completely flat on your back
Identification of the weaker underhook side — the arm with less depth, looser elbow connection, or less secure grip behind your back
Enough remaining energy for the explosive initial wedge insertion — the first two seconds of the attempt are the most demanding
Mental commitment to immediate follow-up — recovering the underhook without transitioning to guard leaves you vulnerable to re-establishment

execution_steps.description: Assess which of the opponent's underhook arms has less depth or a looser elbow connection to their ribcage. The weaker arm is your target — it requires less force to displace and has a higher probability of successful recovery. Feel for the arm that allows slight movement of your leg rather than both being completely locked.
execution_steps.timing: Immediate upon recognizing double unders established

execution_steps.description: Rotate your hips toward the side of the weaker underhook, turning your body approximately thirty degrees off center. This hip angle accomplishes two things: it creates insertion space between their bicep and your thigh on the target side, and it loads your far hip for the subsequent escape movement. Use your free hand on their shoulder or head to assist the rotation.
execution_steps.timing: Within first second of initiating recovery

execution_steps.description: Drive your near-side forearm between the opponent's bicep and your inner thigh on the target side, using a swimming motion from inside to outside. Your elbow leads the insertion, creating a bony wedge that separates their arm from your leg. The forearm must penetrate deep enough that your elbow reaches the crease of their elbow joint, establishing a mechanical block against re-entry.
execution_steps.timing: Explosive insertion during opponent's weight shift or grip adjustment

execution_steps.description: Once your forearm wedge is established, use your other hand to attack their grip connection behind your back. Strip their hand from belt, pants, or gable grip by prying at the weakest point — typically the fingers or the wrist of the displaced arm. Breaking this connection prevents them from immediately re-consolidating the double unders position by removing the anchor point.

Convert your forearm wedge into a proper underhook by threading your arm underneath their displaced arm and securing a grip on their far shoulder or lat. Pull your elbow tight to your own hip to prevent them from swimming back inside. This recovered underhook must be actively maintained with constant inward pressure — any relaxation allows re-pummel to double unders.
execution_steps.timing: Continuous control maintained throughout escape sequence

execution_steps.description: With the underhook secured, execute a sharp hip escape away from the recovered underhook side, sliding your hips out laterally while maintaining elbow-to-hip connection. This shrimp movement creates the space necessary for leg recomposition and prevents the top player from simply re-establishing pressure from a modified angle. Your far leg should begin drawing toward your chest during this movement.

execution_steps.action: Insert knee shield or butterfly hook
execution_steps.description: As the hip escape creates separation, insert your near-side knee as a shield between your hip and their torso, or thread your foot inside their thigh to establish a butterfly hook. The knee shield creates a structural barrier preventing re-engagement of the double unders, while the butterfly hook provides sweep threat that forces the top player to address the guard rather than re-pummel. Prioritize knee shield for immediate security, butterfly hook for offensive transition.
execution_steps.timing: During the hip escape movement, as space opens

execution_steps.description: Complete the transition to a stable guard position by adjusting your leg positioning and grip configuration. For half guard, ensure your bottom leg captures their near leg with a strong knee shield frame maintaining distance. For butterfly guard, insert both hooks and establish collar or sleeve grips. Control their remaining arm or collar to prevent them from immediately re-initiating the passing sequence that led to double unders.
execution_steps.timing: Final consolidation within two to three seconds of underhook recovery

common_counters.counter: Top player immediately re-pummels the displaced arm back to underhook position before you can establish control, using shoulder pressure to override your forearm wedge
common_counters.your_response: Maintain constant inward elbow pressure on recovered underhook and immediately chain into hip escape rather than pausing after wedge insertion — speed of transition defeats re-pummel attempts

common_counters.counter: Top player shifts weight to the opposite side and completes pass around your recovered underhook, using the asymmetry you created to pass on the open side
common_counters.your_response: Follow their weight shift with your hips, using the recovered underhook as a lever to track their movement and recompose guard on the new angle — the underhook gives you connection to follow their direction changes

common_counters.counter: Top player abandons double unders entirely and transitions to a leg drag or toreando pass configuration, using the space you created during recovery to change passing style
common_counters.your_response: The transition to a different passing style gives you time to recompose guard fully — use the moment of position change to establish knee shield or full butterfly guard before they settle into the new passing configuration

common_counters.counter: Top player drives heavy crossface pressure with their head on the recovered underhook side, flattening you back down and neutralizing the angle you created
common_counters.your_response: Frame against their head with your free hand to maintain your hip angle, and use the underhook to pull yourself underneath toward deep half guard entry if they overcommit to crossface pressure — their head pressure creates the angle needed for deep half

common_errors.error: Attempting to recover the underhook on the stronger side where opponent has deeper penetration and tighter elbow connection
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy on a low-percentage attempt, exhausts the arm used for insertion, and allows the top player to advance their pass during your failed recovery effort
common_errors.correction: Always assess both sides before committing — target the arm with shallower depth, looser elbow, or weaker grip connection behind your back

common_errors.error: Recovering the underhook but failing to immediately chain into hip escape and guard recomposition
common_errors.consequence: The top player simply re-pummels the arm back inside within two to three seconds, returning to double unders with your energy depleted from the recovery attempt
common_errors.correction: Treat underhook recovery as step one of a three-part sequence: recover underhook, hip escape, insert knee shield or butterfly hook — all within a continuous two-second window

common_errors.error: Using muscular arm strength to force the forearm wedge rather than proper hip rotation and skeletal alignment
common_errors.consequence: Rapid fatigue of the insertion arm, failed penetration against opponent's connected elbows, and inability to sustain the recovered position
common_errors.correction: Generate insertion force through hip rotation toward the target side — the turning body creates structural separation that muscular effort alone cannot match

common_errors.error: Allowing the elbow to drift away from your hip after recovering the underhook, creating space for opponent to swim back inside
common_errors.consequence: Opponent immediately re-establishes the underhook through the gap between your elbow and hip, returning to double unders without having to overcome any structural barrier
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant elbow-to-hip pressure as a non-negotiable defensive principle — the connection must feel like your elbow is glued to your iliac crest throughout the entire escape sequence

common_errors.error: Attempting the recovery while lying completely flat on your back with no hip angle
common_errors.consequence: No insertion space exists between opponent's arm and your leg when you are flat, making wedge penetration impossible and wasting the attempt
common_errors.correction: Establish at least a thirty-degree hip angle toward the target side before initiating the forearm wedge — use your free hand on their head or shoulder to create this angle first

common_errors.error: Neglecting to strip the opponent's grip behind your back after inserting the forearm wedge
common_errors.consequence: Opponent maintains grip anchor and uses it to pull their displaced arm back into underhook position or transition to a modified control using the remaining connection
common_errors.correction: Dedicate your free hand to breaking their grip connection immediately after the wedge is established — the grip strip and underhook establishment are a coordinated two-hand operation

common_errors.error: Pausing after reaching half guard to rest instead of immediately establishing proper knee shield and grips
common_errors.consequence: Top player immediately initiates knee slice or pressure pass from half guard before you have any defensive structure, negating the entire recovery effort
common_errors.correction: Treat arrival in half guard as the beginning of a new defensive sequence — knee shield, far-side frame, and collar or sleeve control must be established within two seconds of guard recomposition

training_progressions.description: Partner holds light double unders while you practice the forearm wedge insertion on both sides. Focus on identifying the weaker underhook, proper hip rotation to create insertion space, and establishing bone-on-bone contact with the forearm against their bicep. No resistance beyond maintaining the position. Drill thirty repetitions per side per session, emphasizing smooth insertion without muscular forcing.

Partner holds double unders at thirty percent resistance. Practice the complete three-step sequence: recover underhook, hip escape, insert knee shield. Partner allows the recovery but provides light resistance to the hip escape. Focus on eliminating pauses between steps — the sequence must flow as a single continuous motion. Add grip stripping drill to break partner's connection behind your back.

training_progressions.focus: Timing and reaction to pressure changes
training_progressions.description: Partner applies fifty to seventy percent double unders pressure with active weight shifts and grip adjustments. Practice recognizing the optimal timing windows — grip adjustments, weight transfers, breathing pauses — and explosively initiating recovery during those moments. Add the re-pummel counter drill where partner attempts to swim the arm back inside after your initial recovery.

Full resistance positional sparring starting from double unders bottom. Top player works to complete pass while bottom player seeks underhook recovery as one of several escape options. Track success rates and identify which situations favor underhook recovery versus deep half entry or granby roll. Begin chaining failed recovery attempts into secondary escapes.

Integrate underhook recovery into regular rolling sessions with the specific goal of using it whenever double unders are established. Record which passing styles and body types make the technique more or less effective. Develop personalized adjustments based on your body proportions, arm length, and flexibility. Focus on recognizing the double unders threat early and initiating recovery before the position fully consolidates.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of wedging the forearm from inside, use a swimming motion where you reach your arm over their shoulder on the target side and swim it back down inside, using a circular arm path that avoids their connected elbows entirely. Requires more shoulder mobility but bypasses the tightest part of their underhook control.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent has extremely tight elbow connection making direct forearm wedge insertion impossible, or when you have long arms relative to your opponent's torso width

variants_and_adaptations.description: Rather than attacking the underhook directly, use both hands to strip opponent's grip connection behind your back first, separating their gable grip or belt grip with a two-on-one wrist control. Once the grip is broken, their bilateral underhook structure weakens dramatically, making the subsequent forearm wedge insertion significantly easier.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent's grip behind your back is the primary anchor maintaining double unders control, particularly against gable grip configurations where the hands-together connection is the structural keystone

variants_and_adaptations.variant_name: Underhook Recovery to Deep Half Entry
variants_and_adaptations.description: Combine the initial underhook recovery with an immediate deep half guard entry instead of recomposing to standard half guard. After recovering the underhook and creating the hip angle, use the recovered arm to thread underneath opponent's near leg and dive to deep half, using their reaction to the underhook disruption as the entry window.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent responds to your underhook recovery by driving heavy forward pressure to re-establish control — their forward commitment creates the momentum needed for deep half entry underneath their base

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary biomechanical principle that makes underhook recovery effective against double unders control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Double unders derive their crushing power from bilateral symmetry — both arms working in concert to compress the legs and stack the hips. Recovering even a single underhook breaks this symmetry entirely, disrupting the top player's ability to generate equal pressure on both sides. The asymmetry forces them to either abandon the position or fight with only one underhook, which fundamentally changes the dynamic from dominant pressure passing to a contested pummeling exchange where the bottom player has viable defensive options.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent has deep double unders with a tight gable grip behind your back. Which side should you target for the underhook recovery and why?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Target the side where the opponent's elbow sits further from their own ribcage or where their arm has less depth under your leg. With a gable grip, the power hand (palm down) typically has deeper penetration while the secondary hand (palm up) has slightly less structural advantage. Test both sides with subtle hip movements — the side that allows even slight leg movement indicates the weaker underhook. Additionally, target the side where your body angle already favors rotation, which is typically your stronger hip escape direction.

knowledge_assessment.question: You successfully insert your forearm wedge but the opponent immediately begins swimming their arm back inside. What is the critical mechanical detail that prevents re-establishment?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The elbow-to-hip connection is the non-negotiable mechanical block. After inserting the forearm wedge, your elbow must maintain constant pressure against your own iliac crest, creating a closed gate that the opponent's arm cannot pass through. If the elbow drifts even slightly away from your hip, a gap opens that allows their re-pummel. Simultaneously, your free hand must strip their grip behind your back to remove the anchor point that facilitates their re-entry. Both actions together — elbow seal and grip strip — create a structural barrier against re-establishment.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the optimal timing window for initiating the underhook recovery attempt against an active top player?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The highest-percentage windows occur during the opponent's weight shifts and grip adjustments. When they walk their knees forward to advance the pass, momentary lightening of arm pressure occurs as weight transfers to their legs. When they adjust their grip connection behind your back, the bilateral underhook structure briefly weakens. Also effective is timing the attempt to their exhale cycle when chest pressure naturally decreases. The worst time to attempt recovery is during their peak forward drive when both arms are maximally loaded with body weight — this is when the underhook is strongest and wedge insertion most difficult.

knowledge_assessment.question: After recovering the underhook, what are the entry requirements that must exist before you can recompose to half guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Three conditions must be met: the recovered underhook must be secured with elbow-to-hip contact preventing re-pummel, the opponent's grip behind your back must be broken or significantly weakened so they cannot pull the arm back inside, and your hips must have completed at least one hip escape creating lateral separation. Without all three, the half guard recomposition will fail because the top player either re-establishes double unders through the elbow gap, uses their grip to pull you back flat, or simply follows your hips without the lateral space needed for knee shield insertion.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent responds to your underhook recovery by shifting their weight to the opposite side and attempting to pass around your recovered underhook. How do you adjust?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Use the recovered underhook as a tracking handle — because your arm is threaded under theirs, you have a direct connection to follow their lateral movement. Hip escape in the same direction they are moving, pulling yourself toward them with the underhook rather than away. This maintains the connection and allows you to recompose guard on the new angle. The key insight is that your underhook gives you the ability to mirror their movement, so a passing direction change actually becomes easier to defend than direct forward pressure because you can track and follow.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most common failure point in underhook recovery and what is the critical direction of force that must be applied to overcome it?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The most common failure is the forearm wedge failing to penetrate between the opponent's bicep and your thigh. This happens when practitioners push outward (away from their own body) instead of driving inward and downward along the line of their own hip rotation. The critical force direction is lateral and slightly inferior — your hip rotation toward the target side generates the insertion force, while your forearm follows a path parallel to your thigh surface rather than perpendicular to it. Think of sliding your forearm along the groove between their arm and your leg rather than trying to pry them apart.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does underhook recovery differ strategically from a deep half guard entry as an escape from double unders bottom?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Underhook recovery is a conservative option that seeks to return to a neutral guard position with less positional risk, while deep half entry is a committed escape that accepts going deeper underneath the opponent for a higher-reward sweep position. Underhook recovery preserves your current orientation and leads to half guard or butterfly guard, positions you can play defensively. Deep half entry requires rotating your entire body underneath the opponent, which risks being flattened if the entry fails. Choose underhook recovery when you have arm access and moderate pressure, and deep half when the opponent's forward drive is so heavy that using their momentum to dive underneath is the higher-percentage option.

knowledge_assessment.question: What grip configuration should you establish on the opponent's displaced arm after successful underhook recovery to prevent them from re-attacking?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Control the wrist or bicep of the displaced arm with your free hand, pinning it against your chest or steering it toward the mat on the outside of your body. This prevents both the re-pummel to double unders and any crossface attempts. If possible, establish a two-on-one grip momentarily — your underhook arm controlling from underneath while your free hand controls the wrist from on top — creating a complete control circuit on that arm before transitioning to your guard recomposition grips. Release the wrist control only once your knee shield or butterfly hook is securely in place.

knowledge_assessment.question: During live rolling, you notice that larger opponents consistently re-establish double unders despite your underhook recovery attempts. What adaptation addresses this body type disadvantage?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Against significantly larger opponents, modify the approach by prioritizing the two-on-one grip break variant before attempting the forearm wedge. Use both hands to break their grip behind your back first, which weakens the bilateral structure before you challenge the underhook itself. Additionally, increase the hip angle beyond thirty degrees — closer to forty-five — to create more insertion space compensating for their longer arms. Chain immediately into butterfly hook rather than knee shield, as the butterfly hook provides dynamic sweep threat that forces them to address the guard rather than using their size advantage to muscle back to double unders.

safety_considerations: Underhook recovery involves significant shoulder and elbow stress during the forearm wedge insertion phase. The insertion arm experiences compression forces as it penetrates between the opponent's bicep and your thigh — avoid forcing the wedge with a hyperextended wrist, which risks wrist sprains. The recovered underhook shoulder is vulnerable to kimura-type forces if the opponent traps the arm during a failed recovery attempt. If your arm becomes trapped during insertion, immediately abandon the attempt and withdraw rather than fighting through a compromised shoulder position. The stacking pressure inherent to double unders compresses the cervical spine — never bridge explosively while stacked, as this loads the neck dangerously. Train the technique progressively, starting with no resistance to develop clean mechanics before adding pressure. Partners should communicate clearly about neck discomfort during stacking sequences.
position_integration: Underhook Recovery occupies a critical tactical niche in the double unders bottom escape hierarchy. While deep half entry and granby rolls are committed, high-amplitude escapes, underhook recovery provides a moderate-risk pathway back to established guard positions like half guard and butterfly guard. The technique integrates directly into the guard retention chain: when the opponent breaks past your initial guard frames and establishes double unders, underhook recovery serves as the first-line defensive response before resorting to more desperate escape options. Successfully recovered underhooks feed directly into the half guard system where knee shield, underhook sweeps, and back take sequences become available. For practitioners who play pressure passing defense as a primary strategy, underhook recovery is the bridge between losing the guard battle and re-establishing a functional guard position, making it essential for anyone who frequently encounters double unders passing in training or competition.
